title: A Sovereign Country
subtitle: What sovereignty is, and how much of it 1946 actually delivered.
objectives: Explain what sovereignty means in practice
Describe the Philippines' early foreign policy
Explain the role of the bases in sovereignty debates
Judge how sovereignty grew over time

cards.title: Sovereignty is a set of powers, not a feeling
cards.text: A sovereign country decides its own laws, its own trade and its own alliances. In 1946 the Philippines had the first and not much of the others.

cards.title: Four powers that add up to sovereignty
cards.text: Measure a country against these and you get a real answer.
points: **Make its own laws.**
**Control its own borders and defence.**
**Set its own trade and currency.**
**Choose its own allies.**

question.text: Which power did the Philippines have least of in 1946?
options: Setting its own trade and currency
question.explain: The Bell Trade Act fixed trade terms and pegged the peso.

cards.title: Back to the countdown
cards.text: Before 1946 there was 1934. Tap through it again before the two dates.

cards.title: A founding member, and a close alignment
cards.text: The new republic joined the world as an independent voice, and leaned firmly one way.
points: **A founding member of the United Nations** in 1945.
**Closely aligned with the United States** throughout the Cold War.
**Sent troops to Korea** in 1950.
**Hosted the signing of the SEATO treaty** in Manila, 1954.

cards.title: The bases were the sharpest test
cards.text: Foreign troops on your soil is where sovereignty stops being theoretical.
points: **Supporters said** the bases provided defence the country could not afford.
**Critics said** no country is sovereign with foreign forces inside it.
**The agreement was renegotiated** several times and shortened.
**The Senate voted them out in 1991.**

question.text: The Philippines was a founding member of the United Nations.
question.explain: It signed the UN Charter in 1945, before formal independence in 1946.

cards.title: Two independence days, and why both are real
cards.text: The Philippines celebrates 12 June, not 4 July. That was a deliberate choice made in 1962.
points: **12 June 1898** is the declaration by Filipinos themselves.
**4 July 1946** is the date recognition was granted.
**Macapagal moved the holiday** to the earlier date.
**Declared or granted**: the choice of date is an argument about which counts.

cards.title: Sovereignty was gained in pieces
cards.text: Each decade recovered a power that had been limited in 1946.
points: **Parity rights expired** in 1974.
**The peso was unpegged.**
**Base terms were shortened**, then ended in 1991.
**The 1987 Constitution** set out an independent foreign policy.

question.text: When did the Senate vote to end the American bases agreement?
question.explain: In 1991, which is usually taken as the point the last major limit ended.

cards.title: Two circles, one country
cards.alt: Two blank calendar grids side by side, one with a square circled near the top and one near the middle
cards.text: One marks the day it was declared. The other marks the day it was granted.

cards.title: Independence arrives in stages, not in a day
cards.text: It is closer to growing up than to a birthday. Powers are handed over one at a time.
points: **You get some decisions early**, others much later.
**Money is usually the last one.**
**A country is the same.**
**1946 was the start of the process**, not the end.

terms.def: A state's power to govern itself without outside control.
How a country deals with other countries.
A Cold War alliance with its headquarters in Manila.
Consistently siding with one bloc or power.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Sovereignty is laws, borders, trade and alliances together.
In 1946 trade and currency were the weakest of the four.
The Philippines was a UN founding member and closely aligned with the US.
Full sovereignty arrived in pieces, with 1991 the last major step.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 7 Social Studies. Sovereignty is defined as four measurable powers rather than as a feeling, which lets him assess the 1946 settlement himself instead of accepting a verdict. The bases are used as the sharpest test because foreign forces on national soil is where the abstraction becomes concrete, and both sides of that long argument are given their strongest form. The week closes on sovereignty as a staged process ending in 1991, which both corrects the idea that independence was a single day and sets up the later administrations.
discussion: Which four powers add up to sovereignty?
Which did the Philippines have least of in 1946?
Why were the bases the sharpest test?
extension: Score the 1946 republic out of four on the sovereignty powers.
Find out what happened to Clark and Subic after 1991.
misconceptions: That sovereignty is a single thing you either have or do not.
That the bases debate had only one reasonable side.
